newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AWF CUTS AUSTRALIAN WHEAT FORECAST TO 15.3 MT.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AWF CUTS AUSTRALIAN WHEAT FORECAST TO 15.3 MT.

text.p: Private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd (AWF) cut its forecast for Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop to 15.30 million tonnes from its previous estimate of 17.87 million tonnes a month ago.
"Prospects for the Australian wheat crop declined over the past month," AWF managing director Brian Bailey said.

His estimate compares with the Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) latest forecast, issued earlier this week, of 14 million tonnes to 15 million tonnes, down by one million tonnes on its previous prediction.

Australia's official commodities analyst, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE), last put the crop at 16.25 million tonnes, down from the record of 23.5 million tonnes produced in 1996/97.
ABARE's forecast was issued at the beginning of July.
Rainfall was again significantly below average in each of the eastern states, Bailey said.
Crops therefore were stressed for soil moisture, in all areas except where stored soil moisture was available. The soils here were deep and roots had been able to tap the water resource, he said.
In the eastern states the earlier sown crops had grown better and had deeper root systems, he said.
"Crops have now reached a critical stage. Day temperatures are increasing. The leaf area of crops has increased and the amount of water use each day has increased," Bailey said.
The Australian wheat crop was secure for about 10 million to 11 million tonnes, he said.
This was based on six million tonnes from Western Australia and four to five million tonnes from the eastern states.
"To reach our forecast production of 15.3 million tonnes, a number of rains will be needed before October," Bailey said.

The forecast of 1.35 million tonnes production in Queensland was mostly secure as soils were deep and very heavy February rains had occurred, leaving some moisture stored in the soil profile. Grain protein levels from Queensland should be above average, he said.
A similar situation applied for the northern third of New South Wales (NSW). Crops in this third of the state would not fail and would be of high quality, he said.
They would benefit from any further rain during the growing season.
The southern two-thirds of the state had been receiving light rain, but needed at least 50 millimetres of rain in August to avoid crop failure, he said.
Rainfall on Wednesday in the south of the state was helpful, but most totals were only 10-12 mm, he said.
Victorian crops were now stressed in most areas, he said.
About 100,000 hectares in the western Mallee area were intended to be sown to wheat but with continuing dry conditions would not be sown this year, he said.
Rainfall of up to 10 mm on Wednesdasy would keep the poorest crops growing for only another week, he said.
Best Victorian crops were in the southern Wimmera and were sown early on well-prepared fallows, he said.

The South Australian situation was similar to Victoria. But crops in some regions, including the western Eyre Peninsula, Yorke Peninsula, the lower north and the southeast of the state, were already secure from failure.
The wheat should be well filled and of at least normal grain protein, Bailey said.
Western Australian crops were sown early and had received regular rain since germination.
A satisfactory crop was already secure, but some of the crop may be needed for shipment to the eastern states for livestock feeding, he said.
